newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Debt markets close quiet week.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Debt markets close quiet week.

text.p: Asian debt markets closed an uneventful week on a subdued note, with currency uncertainty clouding new issue prospects, bankers said.
In Tokyo, Thanong Bidaya, Thailand's finance minister, said he saw no need for International Monetary Fund (IMF) financing yet for Thailand, despite its currency concerns.
Thanong also said he expected inflation to rise to about six percent from 4.4 percent as a result of the Thai government's decision to float the baht.
He said he would like to see Thai interest rates around 10 percent and that it would not take long for the baht to reach equilibrium.
But the baht's woes are still dampening new issuance activity.
Thai borrowers had already been hit by credit concerns and a sovereign rating downgrade this year,and the currency turmoil has made new issues even more difficult, bankers said this week.
The swap window is a problem, one banker with a European bank said.
Bucking the trend was Thai Farmers Bank, which signed its US$150 million five-year floating-rate certificate of deposit issue. The deal, however, was completed as a club deal.
Thai Farmers also paid an all-in of 42 basis points, against an all-in of 27 basis points that it paid for a five-year U.S. dollar deal in January.

Despite Thanong's assurances on the IMF, a U.S. newspaper reported that both the U.S. Treasury and the IMF are watching the falls in some emerging markets currencies, seeing echoes of the 1994-95 Mexican peso crisis.
"We're certainly in close contact with the IMF, and they're certainly in close contact with the countries that are affected," a U.S. government official was quoted as saying.
The IMF has sent two teams to Thailand to advise on the banking system and currency flotation.
The U.S. newspaper said the IMF's board planned to approve a US$1 billion loan for the Philippines later on Friday, partly to replenish Manila's official reserves after recent sell-offs.
But Philippine central bank governor Gabriel Singson also said on Friday there had been substantial dollar inflows into the Philippines.

In other news, fallout from the Kia rescue plan is pushing out yields on three-year corporate bonds and three month certificates of deposit, despite the Bank of Korea's supply of 989 billion won in emergency funds to the market.
The Bank of Korea has also sold dollars in forward trading to support the won.
Hong Kong property company New World Development Co Ltd is tipped to join the ranks of Hong Kong property companies to be in the market seeking funds, possibly through a five-year loan.
"They're about the only Hong Kong corporate who hasn't refinanced this year," said one banker.
